measure.method: Real Postgres, not arithmetic: PGlite 0.5.15 (PostgreSQL 18.6 compiled to WASM, on-disk dataDir, pg_trgm loaded) taken from the CRM's node_modules and run with node 26 from C:\Users\KHIZAR~1\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\4b2e0699dcdbc578\a8f5ffba-fd8f-465e-b033-54e03564bfec\scratchpad\storage-measure (scripts: gen.cjs generator, lib.cjs DDL, measure_leads.cjs, measure_scale.cjs, measure_other.cjs, project.cjs; results-*.json and projection-table.md kept; scratch DBs deleted). Page layout check: an int4-only table fits 226 rows/page (2,260 rows = 10 pages), identical to a 64-bit server. Steps: (1) 20,000 synthetic leads from a seeded generator whose value lengths and shapes follow the lead bot code (defaults.py 74 headers, leadbot.py row builder, insight.py templates and clips, score.py gap strings, niche pitch templates). (2) LEAN (30 typed fields) and FULL (LEAN + all 74 columns as a jsonb document, non-empty keys only) loaded in 1,000-row batches with all indexes already present (incremental build, the conservative case), then VACUUM (ANALYZE), then pg_total_relation_size = heap + TOAST + FSM/VM + indexes divided by rows. Also measured: FULL with blank keys kept, FULL worst case (all 74 columns at max observed length), and bulk-load-then-CREATE INDEX. (3) Scale check to 100,000 rows (checkpoints 10k/20k/50k/100k) because per-row cost falls with table size. (4) Update churn: 3 status updates per lead, VACUUM after each 20% of rows (emulates default autovacuum), size before vs after. (5) 20,000 rows each for audit_event, sync_log, daily_stats, notification, deletion_request (3-8 lead ids, mean 5) and a slim lead_status_event; plus an EMPTY schema (12 tables, 32 indexes, 9 TOAST tables). (6) project.cjs: monthly model, piecewise-linear lead size through the measured checkpoints, last slope beyond 100k. Per-lead cost used in the projection is therefore the measured curve (about 658 B marginal LEAN, 2,526 B marginal FULL at scale), times the measured churn factor, not the 20k average. Other measured row sizes: deletion_request 499 B (heap 358 + 3 indexes 139), lead_status_event (slim) 129 B. MB = MiB (1,048,576 B); thresholds are APP data (450 MB = Free 500 minus the ~50 MB baseline; 1 GB = 1,024 MB; 8 GB = 8,192 MB).
measure.index_list: LEAD TABLE (both designs; B/row at 20,000 rows, LEAN / FULL): PK(id uuid) 43 / 39; UNIQUE(sheet_id, place_id) 62 / 62; (canonical_email) 46 / 47; (sheet_id, lead_added_on) 11 / 11; (country_code, state) 10 / 11; (niche_id) 11 / 11; (status) 7 / 9; (assigned_to) 9 / 12; GIN pg_trgm on (company) 263 / 279 (falls to 111 / 131 at 100,000 rows; 62 / 74 if built after a bulk load). Index total 464 / 483 B per lead. Trigram judgement: I judge it needed for the search box (employees type a piece of a name; a btree on lower(company) with text_pattern_ops only does starts-with and still costs 45 B/row), but it is the single biggest index: it is 30% of a LEAN lead at 20k rows and 16% at 100k. It can be skipped until about 50k-100k rows (LEAN without it: 603 B at 20k, 589 B at 100k; FULL: 2,450 / 2,440 B). Not included in the planned set: lower(company) btree (measured, then dropped). OTHER TABLES (B/row): audit_event PK(id bigint) 23, (entity_id, ts) 57, (actor_id, ts) 66, BRIN(ts) 1 = 149 index + 530 heap; sync_log PK 23 + (sheet_id, started DESC) 55; daily_stats PK(day, sheet_id, niche_id, country_code) 31 + (sheet_id, day) 13; notification PK 23 + (user_id, created_at DESC) 73; deletion_request PK(uuid) 39 + (status, created_at) 33 + (requested_by, created_at) 67; lead_status_event PK(lead_id, ts) 58 (optional slim table). Small tables: profiles (PK, UNIQUE email), niches (PK, UNIQUE name), sheets (PK, UNIQUE google_sheet_id), tabs (PK, UNIQUE sheet_id+name), sheet_access (PK user_id+sheet_id). Whole schema: 12 tables, 32 indexes, 9 TOAST tables; empty it is 385,024 bytes of relation files (376 KB) and grows pg_database_size by 606,208 bytes (0.58 MB, catalogs included); a bare PG18 database is 7.2 MB (that is not the Supabase ~50 MB baseline, which also holds the auth/storage/realtime schemas). The empty size is the same for LEAN and FULL because LEAN also has a TOAST table.

measure.employee_overhead: Assumptions: 5 employees; every logged action = one audit_event row of 681 B (incl. its 3 indexes; before/after jsonb of about 196 chars each); assignment is a column on the lead plus ONE batch event per assignment, never a row per lead per action; +20 admin/batch events per day (assignments, approvals, edits); month = 30.4 days. Measured result, MB per month for the 5 employees: 100 actions/employee/day = 15,808 events = 10.3 MB/month unpruned (2.1 MB per employee); with 90-day pruning the audit table stops growing at a plateau of 37 MB (3 months x 10.3 x 1.2 bloat allowance). 300/day = 46,208 events = 30.0 MB/month unpruned (6.0 per employee); pruned plateau 108 MB. 1,000/day = 152,608 events = 99.1 MB/month unpruned (19.8 per employee); pruned plateau 357 MB (79% of the Free 450 MB by itself). Other recurring costs that do not depend on employees: sync_log at 5,000 rows/day (10 sheets x about 500 logged scans) = 23.2 MB/month unpruned, plateau 27.9 MB with 30-day pruning; notifications at 100/day = 0.98 MB/month; deletion requests at 10/day = 0.14 MB/month; daily_stats 0.25-0.95 MB/month (at most 270 rows/day x 122 B). Status history: 3 events per NEW lead stored as audit rows = 2,043 B per lead, which is 2.4 times the LEAN lead row itself; a slim lead_status_event table (129 B per event) would make it 386 B. Backlog leads get no history at import (a sheet stores only the current status); their later changes are the employee actions counted above. If you also charged 3 events to each of 50,000 backlog leads it would add about 97 MB once (gone after 90 days when pruned). Key finding: below about 5,000 new leads/month, logging (sync_log + audit) is the main storage cost, not the leads. 5 employees assigned everything add one column (assigned_to, 9 B/row of index) and nothing else per lead.

ANSWER TO 'HOW LONG TO FILL 500 MB' using the bot's own volume estimate (about 10,000 leads in month 1, then about 2,500/month; 5 employees at 300 actions/day, no backlog): LEAN not pruned = 450 MB in 6.9 months, 1 GB in 16.3, 8 GB in 133 (11.1 y); month 12 = 761 MB. LEAN pruned = 450 MB in 90 months (7.5 y), 1 GB in 271 (22.6 y), 8 GB never in practice; month 12 = 202 MB, month 24 = 240 MB. FULL not pruned = 450 MB in 6.1 months, 1 GB in 14.7; month 12 = 845 MB. FULL pruned = 450 MB in 31 months (2.6 y), 1 GB in 96 (8.0 y), 8 GB in 914 (76 y); month 12 = 287 MB, month 24 = 392 MB. Reading: at the bot's real volume, 500 MB is lasting for years ONLY if audit (90 d) and sync_log (30 d) are pruned; without pruning the logs, not the leads, fill it in 6-7 months. A 1 GB free database buys roughly double the time. Sensitivities: if sync_log writes only on change or error (about 1,000 rows/day) LEAN 2,500/month not pruned reaches 450 MB in 10.4 months instead of 7.3 (FULL 9.2 instead of 6.6); with the slim 129 B status-history table instead of audit rows, LEAN 20,000/month not pruned reaches 450 MB in 5.8 months instead of 4.1. If the 50 MB baseline is also counted against the 1 GB and 8 GB lines, subtract about 0.1-0.8 months from the 1 GB column.
caveats: NO real lead data: fill rates are assumptions (45.8 of 74 columns non-empty) and lengths come from the bot code; the only lead CSV on disk is a different automation (job-board leads) and was used for a text-length cross-check only (its Lead Insight is shorter: mean 128 vs my 269). Re-measure with the pilot sheets: run select pg_total_relation_size('leads')/count(*) after the first import.

PGlite is PostgreSQL 18.6 on 32-bit WASM; Supabase runs 15 or 17. Page layout verified identical (226 int4 rows per 8 KB page), pglz is the default TOAST compression in both, so expect within a few percent. Not tested: lz4 TOAST compression, which could shrink the FULL jsonb. Run-to-run variation of two identical runs was 0.2-0.7% (random uuids), churn 1.143 to 1.154.

Per-row cost falls with table size, so the 20k figures overstate large tables: LEAN 867 B/row at 20k, 700 at 100k, marginal 658 beyond 50k; FULL 2,729 / 2,571 / marginal 2,526. The trigram GIN index is the reason (263 B/row at 20k, 111 at 100k) and depends on how diverse real company names are (+-30%); my synthetic names come from a small vocabulary. The projection uses the measured curve, not the 20k average. Built after a bulk load instead of row-by-row the GIN index is 62 B/row at 20k, so REINDEX after the backlog import saves about 25% of LEAN (634 vs 867 B at 20k).

Update churn is included: 3 status updates per lead with autovacuum emulated by a VACUUM after every 20% of rows gives LEAN x1.143 (heap +20%, indexes +9%) and FULL x1.226 (the raw jsonb is rewritten on each status change, so TOAST grows 31%). It plateaus after the first pass, but only while autovacuum keeps up (default 20%); the status index prevents HOT updates. Keeping the raw jsonb in a separate table that is not rewritten on status-only changes would give FULL the LEAN churn factor.

Status history is the biggest per-lead cost when stored as audit rows: 3 x 681 B = 2,043 B per lead, more than the LEAN lead itself (867 B). The projection charges it as audit rows as requested; a slim table (129 B per event, measured) cuts it to 386 B. Backlog leads are charged no history (see employee_overhead for the +97 MB if you charge them).

sync_log is assumed at 5,000 rows/day (10 sheets x about 500 logged scans) and that alone is 23.2 MB/month; the real figure depends on what the scanner logs. Pruned tables are given +20% bloat because DELETE frees space for reuse but never shrinks the file; monthly partitions (drop a partition) avoid it. VACUUM FULL or pg_repack is needed to give disk back.

Thresholds are app data in MiB: the ~50 MB Supabase baseline is not included, WAL is not counted, and only the 12 planned tables were measured (no Storage objects, no auth.users, no pg_cron history, no Realtime). A 1 GB or 8 GB plan changes only the threshold, not the growth.

Measured variants beyond the two requested: FULL with blank keys kept = 2,934 B/lead (+7%); FULL worst case with all 74 columns at their maximum observed length = 5,035 B/lead (+85%). The AU-only edition has 82 columns; the 8 extra keys add an estimated 150-200 B of jsonb per AU-only lead (estimated from lengths, not measured).

Synthetic text is built from a 1,413-word vocabulary (taken from the lead-bot docs) with Zipf-like weights, so compressibility is similar to English prose but real scraped text could differ by +-10% in the FULL TOAST size. No concurrency, no replication slots and no index bloat from deletes were modelled; the ix_status and ix_assigned indexes are plain (not partial), which is the conservative choice.

Nothing under F:\Github Repos was edited and no secret files were opened. Only non-secret docs of the lead bot (CONTRACT.md, SHEETS_SETUP.md, README.md, UPGRADE_V3-V5.md) were read to build the word list, plus the source files named in the task.

pgs.notes:
BOTTOM LINE (my judgment, not a sourced fact): free + at least 1 GB + no expiry exists at only four providers: Neon (1 GB per project, but only 100 CU-hours so it cannot run a 1-minute scanner 24/7), Prisma Postgres (2 GB but 200k operations per month, evaluation-only), Aiven (1 GB, always-on VM, bare Postgres, not for production) and Nile (1 GB, always-on, no backups, tenant model). Render (30-day expiry), Koyeb (5 h compute and paid signup), Railway/Fly/Heroku (no free DB), CockroachDB (free closed 2026-09-15), Xata (no free plan), Tiger Data (about 750 MB, beta) and Vercel (just a wrapper) fail. None of them gives the Supabase bundle (Auth + Realtime + Edge Functions + pg_cron) with 1 GB free, so choosing any of them means rebuilding Auth, single-session, emailed reset, Realtime and the scanner scheduler yourself. Supabase (not in my list, one source only, Voroa 2026-10-16: 500 MB, paused after 1 week of low activity, not paused if the 1-minute scanner keeps it active) remains the only full-stack fit; a Neon+Aiven hybrid is possible but is a rewrite.

CONFLICTS FLAGGED: Neon storage is 1 GB per project since 2026-10-02 (official pricing, plans docs, blog, changelog, Voroa agree); selfhost.dev, Bytebase, cloudinsight and some search snippets still say 0.5 GB and are stale. Prisma Postgres: official pricing page says 2 GB / 200k ops / 50 DBs; Voroa and older PR diffs show 500 MB / 100k ops (stale). CockroachDB: srvrlss.io still lists the free allowance, contradicted by the official pricing notice 'Such pricing is no longer available for purchase'. Koyeb: older official FAQ/docs still mention a free Starter plan; the pricing page and trackers say it is closed to new users since Feb 2026 (exact date 2026-02-26 is from agentdeals only).

NOT VERIFIED / SKIPPED: (1) Tiger Data 750 MB is not printed on any official page I could read (marked partly). (2) Commercial-use clauses are mostly 'not stated' on vendor pages; I did not read each provider's full ToS or master agreement. (3) Aiven inactivity period and whether a 1-minute job prevents power-off are not published. (4) Auth/Realtime/cron coverage for Prisma Postgres, Tiger Data and Nile (pg_cron) is 'not found', not 'confirmed absent'. (5) Operation and CU-hour estimates for this app are my arithmetic from stated assumptions (11 sheets, one sync per minute), not measured. (6) Supabase itself was out of scope and not independently verified. Page text was summarised by a small model; key numbers were cross-checked across multiple pages, but quote-level wording should be re-read before publishing. All dates checked: 2026-11-04.

others.group: Non-Postgres and infrastructure free-tier options for the Database lead-tracking app (all figures checked 2026-11-04)

providers.plan: Spark (no-cost) plan, Firestore Standard edition
providers.free_storage: 1 GiB total stored data; exactly one free database per project. Meets the 1 GB floor on size alone.
providers.expiry_pause_or_deletion: No idle pause or deletion rule found on the pages read. Google says the Free Tier has no end date but may change it with 30 days notice. Daily quotas reset about midnight Pacific.
providers.sql_postgres: No. NoSQL document database. Only count/sum/avg aggregation queries, no SQL, no joins.
providers.other_free_limits: 50K reads/day, 20K writes/day, 20K deletes/day, 10 GiB/month egress. Cloud Functions are 'Not applicable' on Spark (every function metric is blank), so no server code at all without upgrading to Blaze. Enterprise edition on Spark: 40K write units/day, 50K read units/day, 50K realtime update units/day.
providers.backups: None free. Firestore quotas page: PITR, backup, restore and clone have no free usage and need billing.

providers.has_auth_realtime_cron: Realtime listeners and Firebase Auth exist (known capability, not re-checked today). Per-collection access rules exist (Security Rules). Scheduled jobs and any server-side session revocation are blocked on Spark because Cloud Functions are unavailable.
providers.fit_for_this_app: Poor. 20K writes/day against roughly 7,920 (2-min) to 15,840 (1-min) sync cycles/day across 11 sheets (computed): one refresh of a 2,000-row sheet would use 10% of the day's writes. No scheduled scanner on Spark, no SQL aggregates, no emailed-code reset flow built in (Firebase uses reset links; not re-checked). Would need a full rewrite and a paid Blaze plan to work.

providers.plan: Workers Free plan
providers.free_storage: 5 GB total per account across at most 10 databases, BUT 500 MB maximum per database on Free (paid: 10 GB per database). A single database cannot reach 1 GB; you would have to shard into 2+ databases.
providers.expiry_pause_or_deletion: No idle pause or deletion found. Daily limits reset 00:00 UTC; after hitting a daily limit queries are refused until reset. When storage is full, inserts and schema changes are blocked (tracker, not Cloudflare wording).
providers.sql_postgres: SQL, but SQLite dialect, not Postgres.
providers.other_free_limits: 5M rows read/day, 100K rows written/day, 10 databases, 50 queries per Worker invocation (a db.batch() counts as one). Workers Free: 100K requests/day, 10 ms CPU per request and per cron run, 5 Cron Triggers per account, 50 subrequests.
providers.backups: Time Travel point-in-time restore, 7 days on Free (30 days paid).
providers.commercial_use_ok: Not verified (terms not read).
providers.has_auth_realtime_cron: No built-in auth, no row-level security, no realtime push. D1 is only reachable from Workers (or the REST API). Cron: Workers Cron Triggers (5 per account, 10 ms CPU each). Durable Objects on Free not verified.
providers.fit_for_this_app: Poor to partial. Storage per database fails the 1 GB request. 100K row-writes/day is enough only if the mirror writes diffs, not full sheets. You would have to build auth, per-sheet access rules, single-session control, emailed reset codes and realtime counters yourself in Workers, and cross-database aggregates are not possible if sharded.

providers.plan: Free plan (no credit card)
providers.free_storage: 5 GB total, up to 100 databases.

A Turso blog post (effective 2025-03-31) says free databases stay responsive regardless of inactivity. Treat as unresolved; a 1-minute scanner would keep the database active anyway. providers.sql_postgres: SQL, SQLite/libSQL dialect, not Postgres.

providers.plan: Open source, MIT license; runs on your own free host
providers.free_storage: No vendor cap: one SQLite file (pb_data) on the host disk. Free hosts that persist disk: Oracle Always Free (200 GB block+boot combined) and Google Cloud e2-micro (30 GB standard disk, 1 GB RAM, US regions only). Render free has an ephemeral filesystem and spins down after 15 minutes idle; Fly.io has no free tier for new orgs ($1 credit for 7 days, volumes $0.15/GB/month).

providers.sql_postgres: SQLite embedded; no client-side SQL. Aggregates need custom routes or hooks.
providers.other_free_limits: Single process on one VM, so no high availability. May need raised file-descriptor limit for many realtime connections; GOMEMLIMIT advised on small hosts.
providers.backups: Built-in full ZIP backups of pb_data (scheduled), stored locally or on S3-compatible storage; performance dips during backup.
providers.commercial_use_ok: Yes on the code side: MIT license (verified on GitHub). Host terms separate.
providers.has_auth_realtime_cron: Built-in users/auth (OTP and MFA per production docs), collection API rules (row-level filters), realtime subscriptions, JS hooks and a jobs-scheduling feature (cron page exists, content not read). Single active session per login is not built in; needs a custom hook.
providers.fit_for_this_app: Medium. Everything lives in one free binary and storage is no issue, but it is SQLite and PocketBase rules, not Postgres RLS, so the CRM/Outreach code patterns do not carry over. Status risks: pre-1.0 (latest v0.40.6 on 2026-10-23), docs say not recommended for production-critical apps, and the GitHub repo is now ARCHIVED with a README notice that development moved to ganigeorgiev.com (verified via GitHub API; link not followed).

providers.plan: Always Free, up to 2 databases per tenancy
providers.free_storage: 20 GB per database (2 databases = 40 GB), 1 fixed OCPU, cannot be scaled.
providers.expiry_pause_or_deletion: Auto-stops after 7 days of inactivity (data kept; a SQL connection resets the timer). providers.sql_postgres: SQL, Oracle dialect (19c or 26ai), not Postgres.

providers.commercial_use_ok: Not stated on the pages read; not verified.

providers.fit_for_this_app: Poor. Large free storage, but Oracle SQL means rewriting everything, there is no backup/restore (a data-loss risk for a lead tracker), and the HTTP layer tops out around 3-6 simultaneous users.

providers.provider: Oracle Cloud Arm VM (Always Free) + self-hosted Supabase or Postgres
providers.plan: Always Free Ampere A1 compute + block storage
providers.free_storage: 200 GB combined boot+block volume, 5 volume backups total, 2 OCPU and 12 GB RAM across A1 instances (1,500 OCPU-hours and 9,000 GB-hours/month; halved from 4 OCPU/24 GB in 2026 without announcement per InfoQ/heise/Oracle docs). A Supabase stack idling near 3 GB of 12 GB RAM would likely be above 20% memory (inference, not Oracle-confirmed). Over-allocated A1 instances are disabled and deleted after 30 days. Unresolved: Site2US cites an Oracle FAQ saying accounts idle 30+ days may be suspended; Oracle docs read do not mention it. Anecdotal reports of sudden account termination exist. A1 capacity is sometimes unavailable at creation.
providers.sql_postgres: Full Postgres if you self-host (plain Postgres or the Supabase Docker stack).
providers.other_free_limits: Supabase self-host minimum is 4 GB RAM, 2 cores, 40 GB SSD (8 GB+, 4 cores, 80 GB recommended); 2 OCPU/12 GB meets it. Docs do not state arm64 support for all images and do not mention pg_cron on self-host; both must be tested. Stack includes Auth, Realtime, Edge Functions (Deno), Storage. You own TLS, secrets, monthly stable-snapshot updates, monitoring.
providers.backups: Self-managed (pg_dump to off-box storage or the 20 GB object storage); only 5 volume backups free.
providers.commercial_use_ok: Not stated on the Oracle pages read; not verified.
providers.has_auth_realtime_cron: Yes if you run the full Supabase stack: Postgres + Auth + Realtime + Edge Functions; scheduling via pg_cron/pg_net is documented for hosted Supabase and must be tested on self-host.
providers.fit_for_this_app: Best technical match for a free 1 GB+ requirement: same stack as the CRM and Outreach apps, up to roughly 150 GB usable, RLS and realtime intact. Costs: single-VM availability, reclaim and termination risk, arm64 and pg_cron unverified, and you carry all operations and backups. Worth a 1-day pilot before committing.

providers.other_free_limits: Cloud Run 2M requests/month, Cloud Run functions (1st gen) 2M invocations/month, Pub/Sub 10 GiB/month, Firestore 50K reads/20K writes/20K deletes per day.
providers.backups: Not provided for free tier resources on the pages read.
providers.commercial_use_ok: Not verified (terms not read). Usage over limits is billed to the card.
providers.has_auth_realtime_cron: Components exist separately (Cloud Run, Pub/Sub, Firestore listeners) but nothing is integrated; Cloud Scheduler free status not found.
providers.fit_for_this_app: Poor as a managed option. The e2-micro's 1 GB RAM is too small for Supabase (needs 4 GB) but could host plain Postgres or PocketBase with 30 GB; otherwise the Firestore limits apply.

providers.provider: AWS DynamoDB (always-free allowance) and AWS Free Plan rules
providers.plan: Always-free monthly allowance; new accounts (since 2025-07-15) choose Free plan or Paid plan
providers.free_storage: DynamoDB: 25 GB storage, 25 provisioned WCU, 25 provisioned RCU, 25 rWCU, 2.5M Streams read requests, 1 GB data transfer out per month (per Region, per payer account; provisioned capacity, Standard table class). Lambda 1M requests and 400K GB-seconds also always free. RDS, EC2, S3 and API Gateway are not on the always-free list; they draw down credits.

BUT a Free-plan account closes after 6 months or when its $100 sign-up credit (plus up to $100 earned) is used, whichever is first; data is retained 90 days, then deleted unless you upgrade to a Paid plan (pay-as-you-go, card). Storage over 25 GB costs $0.25/GB-month in the page's examples.
providers.sql_postgres: No. NoSQL key-value/document. SQL-like PartiQL only; no joins or SQL aggregates.
providers.other_free_limits: Trackers estimate roughly 200M requests/month from 25 RCU/WCU (not an AWS statement).
providers.backups: PITR is not free: $0.20 per GB-month; restore $0.15/GB (pricing page example).
providers.commercial_use_ok: Not verified (terms not read).
providers.has_auth_realtime_cron: Not integrated. Cron via EventBridge/Lambda and auth via Cognito are separate services whose free limits were not verified here; no row-level SQL security; realtime would need Streams plus another service.
providers.fit_for_this_app: Poor. 25 GB is plentiful, but it needs a full rewrite to NoSQL, assembling 4+ AWS services for auth, realtime and scheduling, and the account must be upgraded to Paid after 6 months to survive.

providers.plan: Monthly free allowance (applied to the bill automatically)
providers.free_storage: 1 GB-month storage and 100,000 DPUs per month, per account (per management account in AWS Organizations). Exactly at the 1 GB floor; beyond it you are billed ($0.33/GB-month, $8 per million DPUs in US East), not blocked.
providers.expiry_pause_or_deletion: AWS pages give no end date (third-party trackers call it permanent; AWS wording not found). Storage is billed even when idle. Interaction with the 6-month Free-plan account closure is not verified.
providers.sql_postgres: Postgres-compatible SQL. Per AWS docs: no triggers, no PL/pgSQL, no temporary tables, no TRUNCATE (use DELETE), one built-in database per cluster, C collation only, Repeatable Read only, a transaction can change at most 3,000 rows, connections time out after 1 hour, optimistic concurrency with retries. Extensions (pg_cron), row-level security and LISTEN/NOTIFY are not confirmed by the pages read.
providers.other_free_limits: AWS benchmark: 100K DPUs is about 700,000 TPC-C transactions; whether 11 sheets mirrored every 1-2 minutes plus a 1-minute scanner fit is not computable from published numbers.
providers.backups: Not stated on the pages read.
providers.commercial_use_ok: Not verified.
providers.has_auth_realtime_cron: No built-in auth (IAM-token connections), no realtime, no scheduler.
providers.fit_for_this_app: Poor. Postgres-like but missing triggers, PL/pgSQL and (unconfirmed) RLS, a 3,000-row transaction cap complicates bulk sheet mirrors, and every Supabase feature (Auth, Realtime, cron) would have to be rebuilt on AWS.

providers.plan: Free tier, General Purpose serverless, lifetime of the subscription (not the 12-month free account)
providers.free_storage: Per database per month: 32 GB data, 32 GB backup storage, 100,000 vCore-seconds; up to 10 free databases per subscription.
providers.expiry_pause_or_deletion: Not time-limited. Choose at the limit: AutoPause (database inaccessible until the next calendar month) or bill overage (cannot switch back). Database also auto-pauses after 15 minutes idle (fixed). Open connections block auto-pause. No SLA; Microsoft recommends it mainly for dev/proof of concept. Free tier only on new databases, not convertible.
providers.sql_postgres: SQL, T-SQL (SQL Server dialect), not Postgres.
providers.other_free_limits: 100,000 vCore-seconds is only 27.8 vCore-hours (computed). A 1-minute scanner keeps the database awake, so the allowance lasts about 1.2 days at 1 vCore or 2.3 days at 0.5 vCore (computed; minimum vCore for the free offer not verified), after which AutoPause locks the app out until next month.
providers.backups: Point-in-time restore up to 7 days on AutoPause setting, locally redundant; no long-term retention. Elastic Jobs and Data Sync not available.
providers.commercial_use_ok: Microsoft FAQ: no SLA, recommended primarily for development and proof-of-concept; otherwise not stated.
providers.has_auth_realtime_cron: None integrated. Elastic Jobs unavailable on free; scheduling would be Azure Functions or similar (limits not verified).
providers.fit_for_this_app: Fail for an always-on workload: compute allowance is exhausted in days. Also T-SQL rewrite and no auth/realtime/RLS parity.

providers.free_storage: First 1,000 RU/s and 25 GB storage free for the life of the account; one free-tier account per subscription. Usage above that is billed at normal prices (not blocked).
providers.expiry_pause_or_deletion: No expiry for the account's discount. Pricing page's billing FAQ is inconsistent (mentions 400 RU/s and 5 GB 'each month'); the free-tier page and pricing page headline say 1,000 RU/s and 25 GB.
providers.sql_postgres: NoSQL (document API); not SQL aggregates comparable to Postgres.
providers.other_free_limits: Shared-throughput database limited to 1,000 RU/s free, max 25 containers. Egress still billed per one guide.
providers.backups: Not verified for the free tier.
providers.commercial_use_ok: Microsoft says free tier can run small production workloads; terms not otherwise verified.
providers.has_auth_realtime_cron: No app auth or row-level rules; change feed gives a realtime source only via extra code; scheduling needs Azure Functions (limits not verified).
providers.fit_for_this_app: Poor. Plenty of storage, but a NoSQL rewrite with every Supabase capability to be rebuilt, and 1,000 RU/s is tight for continuous sheet mirroring.

others.notes:
BOTTOM LINE (checked 2026-11-04): No non-Postgres managed free tier is a good fit. Only two routes give at least 1 GB free AND the full auth + row-level access + realtime + scheduler + SQL aggregate set: (1) self-host Supabase or Postgres on the Oracle Always Free Arm VM (2 OCPU, 12 GB RAM, 200 GB disk; best match, but you carry operations, backups, and Oracle reclaim/termination risk; arm64 images and pg_cron on self-host are unverified, so pilot first), or (2) stay on hosted Supabase Free at 500 MB (not re-verified in this pass; belongs to the Postgres research agent). Managed options with 1 GB or more of free storage each fail on something else: Turso (5 GB, SQLite, database only, no auth/RLS/realtime/cron), D1 (5 GB per account but 500 MB per database), Azure SQL free (32 GB but 100,000 vCore-seconds/month runs out in days), Oracle Autonomous DB (20 GB, Oracle SQL, no backups), Aurora DSQL (exactly 1 GB, missing triggers/PL/pgSQL), Firestore (1 GiB but 20K writes/day and no scheduled jobs on Spark), DynamoDB/Cosmos (NoSQL rewrite, DynamoDB account closes after 6 months on the Free plan). Below 1 GB or paused: MongoDB M0 512 MB, Convex 0.5 GB, Back4App 250 MB, Appwrite (2 GB but pauses after 1 week idle, deletes after 90 days paused).

WORKLOAD MATH USED (computed, not from vendors): 11 sheets mirrored every 2 min = 7,920 sync cycles/day; every 1 min = 15,840/day; a 1-minute scanner = 1,440 runs/day = 43,200/month.

NOTES ON EVIDENCE: A source counts if I read the page or a search result attributed the figure to it; official pages listed first. 'partly' on Appwrite because DB read/write quotas and the cron-needs-paid-plan rule rest on one third-party tracker (agentdeals.dev); its 2 GB, 1-week pause and 90-day deletion are confirmed on appwrite.io. Commercial-use terms (ToS) were NOT read for any provider; every 'Not verified' there is deliberate. Conflicts left unresolved: Turso free-plan archiving after 10 days idle (docs) vs 'always responsive' (blog); MongoDB M0 backups (docs say yes, pricing FAQ says no); Oracle account-idle suspension window (30 days per one third-party page citing the FAQ, not in the Oracle docs read); Cosmos DB billing FAQ numbers. Oracle's A1 allowance was cut to 2 OCPU/12 GB in 2026; older guides and one search summary still say 4/24. Whether Pay-As-You-Go tenancies are exempt is disputed (InfoQ).

OTHER FINDINGS WORTH KNOWING: (a) PocketBase GitHub repo is archived (confirmed via GitHub API) with a README notice that the project moved to ganigeorgiev.com; latest release v0.40.6 (2026-10-23), still pre-1.0 and the docs say not recommended for production-critical apps. I did not follow the new link. (b) Supabase announced on 2026-10-02 it is acquiring Turso (Turso blog, SiliconANGLE); free-tier continuity not promised. (c) One secondary source (layerbase.com via search summary) says Neon doubled its free storage to 1 GB per project on 2026-10-02; this is outside my scope and unverified, so the Postgres research agent should check it first-hand because it would meet the 1 GB request with a Postgres database. (d) No file in F:\Github Repos was touched and no secrets files were opened.

supa.group: Supabase specifics: Free plan limits, Pro, upgrade path, size reduction, programs, and self-hosting (Hetzner / Oracle). Checked 2026-11-04.

providers.provider: Supabase Free: what happens past 500 MB (questions 1 and 6 baseline)
providers.plan: Free, $0. 2 active free projects. Nano compute (shared CPU, up to 0.5 GB RAM).
providers.free_storage: 500 MB database-size quota. Per the current docs it is a billing quota for the organisation (summed over all projects in the org), not a disk limit. Free disk is fixed at 2 GB and does not autoscale. A fresh project already uses about 40-60 MB (extensions, default schemas), so about 440-460 MB is usable. Also 1 GB file storage and 5 GB egress.
providers.expiry_pause_or_deletion: Nothing is deleted at 500 MB. Order of events per the official docs: (a) email notice plus a grace period; the length is NOT published (user-posted notices show roughly 2-3 weeks, e.g. notice 3 Nov 2025 with grace to 26 Nov 2025; another ended 10 Nov 2026). (b) After grace, if the org is still over quota, a Fair Use restriction: every API request for ALL projects in the org returns HTTP 402. The check uses the AVERAGE daily DB size over the billing cycle, so deleting data does not lift it at once; it clears when the quota refills next cycle, or immediately on upgrade to Pro or by disabling the spend cap (Pro only). Users report 402 lingering up to about 24h after a cycle reset (Discussion 46758, June 2026). (c) Read-only mode is a separate, disk-based trigger: at 95% of the 2 GB disk the DB goes read-only (writes fail with SQLSTATE 25006) and returns to read-write once usage is under 95%; at 100% Postgres stops until you upgrade. To free a read-only DB: run set session characteristics as transaction read write, delete, vacuum, then set default_transaction_read_only off. CONFLICT: the docs said read-only at 500 MB until a fix merged on 13 Apr 2026 (issue 43487, PR 44457), and third-party blogs dated as late as 7 Oct 2026 still say read-only at 500 MB. Plan for both outcomes. Separately, Free projects are paused after more than a week of too little database activity (never on Pro); restore window is not stated on the official FAQ (third-party says 90 days older / 1 year newer: not verified). Free has no automatic backups.
providers.other_free_limits: Unused-for-a-week pause; 5 GB egress; 50,000 MAU; storage 1 GB; no backups; no SLA. Disk does not shrink after deletes unless vacuumed or the project is upgraded or migrated.
providers.has_auth_realtime_cron: Yes: Auth, Realtime, Edge Functions and pg_cron (Supabase Cron runs jobs from every second to once a year; docs recommend at most 8 concurrent jobs, each under 10 minutes).
providers.sql_postgres: Real Postgres (Supabase managed), full SQL and RLS.
providers.backups: None on Free. Docs tell Free users to export regularly with the CLI db dump command. Pro gets daily backups kept 7 days.
providers.commercial_use_ok: No Free-plan commercial ban found in the Terms of Service or Acceptable Use Policy; a community answer (not staff, Feb 2024) says allowed. Supabase recommends Pro for production. Not officially stated, so partly.
providers.fit_for_this_app: Works only while average DB size stays under 500 MB. Set an alert at about 350 MB (pg_database_size) and treat 402 as app-down. A 1-minute pg_cron scanner also writes to cron.job_run_details (never auto-cleaned), so add a daily cleanup job. Note: the user's CRM (ref laxxqmtwowitopbqnejs) and Outreach (ref bnivytzudrpjlscwdxuh) are both recorded as Free projects in their project CLAUDE.md files, so a third Free project is not allowed on the same account (see the upgrade entry).

providers.provider: Supabase Free: Storage bucket 1 GB for nightly compressed snapshots (question 3)
providers.plan: Free, file storage (S3-backed buckets)
providers.free_storage: 1 GB total (744 GB-hours, billed as an average over the cycle). Max 50 MB per file on Free (the global file-size limit cannot be set above 50 MB; Pro can go up to 500 GB). This quota is separate from the 500 MB database quota. Pro: 100 GB, then $0.0213/GB/month.
providers.expiry_pause_or_deletion: Files are not auto-deleted. Over 1 GB on Free: email, grace period, then the same Fair Use restriction (HTTP 402 for the whole org); Free has no pay-per-use overage. Because it is an average, cutting storage late in the cycle clears the restriction only slowly. Staff note (Nov 2025): delete through the Storage API or UI, not by deleting rows in storage.objects with SQL.
providers.other_free_limits: Project pause after a week of inactivity applies. Storage image transformations cost extra on paid plans.
providers.has_auth_realtime_cron: Part of the same project: signed uploads via service role from an Edge Function or pg_cron plus pg_net, or from any external script.
providers.sql_postgres: Object metadata lives in storage.objects (tiny rows count toward DB size).
providers.backups: Storage objects are not part of the DB backups; this entry IS the backup target.
providers.commercial_use_ok: Same as Free plan.
providers.fit_for_this_app: Yes, with two limits. (1) 50 MB per file: a nightly pg_dump custom format (-Fc, already compressed) or .sql.gz must be under 50 MB or be split into parts of 45 MB or less. (2) 1 GB total: about 7 daily snapshots of up to about 140 MB, or 20 of 45 MB. Compression ratio for lead data is my estimate, NOT measured: test with pg_dump on the real DB. Weakness: same vendor and account, so it is not a true off-site backup; keep one weekly copy elsewhere (Drive/R2/B2, not verified here).

providers.provider: Supabase Pro (questions 4 and 7: cost, what 8 GB gives, spend cap)
providers.plan: Pro, from $25/month per organisation plus usage. Spend cap ON by default.
providers.free_storage: 8 GB database disk per project included (16x the Free 500 MB), then $0.125/GB/month on the default gp3 disk. Also 100 GB file storage (then $0.0213/GB), 250 GB egress, 100,000 MAU, daily backups kept 7 days. $10/month compute credit covers one Micro project (1 GB RAM shared CPU, about $10/month); each extra project in the org costs about $10/month more (Small about $15). Autoscaling: disk grows 50% when it reaches 90% full (cap 200 GB, at most 4 changes per rolling 24h, one per 4h), but going past 8 GB needs the spend cap turned OFF.
providers.expiry_pause_or_deletion: No inactivity pausing, no expiry. With the spend cap on, usage over quota is restricted rather than billed; turning it off lifts any restriction immediately and switches to pay-as-you-go. A new Pro compute change (Nano to Micro) restarts the DB, usually under 2 minutes.
providers.other_free_limits: PITR add-on is expensive: about $100/month (7 days), $200 (14), $400 (28). Daily backups are included without it.
providers.has_auth_realtime_cron: Yes: Auth, Realtime, Edge Functions, pg_cron, same as Free.
providers.sql_postgres: Real Postgres, full SQL and RLS.
providers.backups: Daily backups, 7-day retention; PITR optional add-on (about $100/month for 7 days).
providers.commercial_use_ok: Yes (paid production plan).
providers.fit_for_this_app: Best fit if the user wants no maintenance: about $25/month (one project, Micro covered by the credit) gives 8 GB, backups, and no pausing. If the CRM and Outreach projects live in the same org they all become Pro and extra projects add about $10/month each (about $45/month for three, matching the selfhost.dev example); to avoid that, keep them in a separate Free org. 8 GB at the other agent's measured bytes per lead is the number to divide by for time-to-fill.

providers.provider: Supabase: upgrade or move a Free project in place (question 5)
providers.plan: Free to Pro via the organisation billing settings; Project Transfers between organisations
providers.free_storage: Same project, same data, same ref and region; the plan belongs to the ORGANISATION, so every project in that org becomes Pro when it is upgraded. A Pro and a Free project cannot share an org. To keep some projects free, put them in a separate Free org (project transfer: Project Settings, General; you must own the source org and be a member of the target; no GitHub integration or log drains; same region only).
providers.expiry_pause_or_deletion: Upgrade does not delete or pause anything. Downtime of the plan switch itself is not stated in the official docs (one third-party guide says zero; not verified). Compute stays Nano (billed like Micro on a paid org) until you resize to Micro, which restarts the DB (usually under 2 minutes, can run longer; one 2-hour outage was reported during a failed resize in sa-east-1). Moving a project from a paid org to a Free org may cause 1-2 minutes of downtime and checks the 2-free-project limit.
providers.other_free_limits: FLAG: the 2-free-project limit counts across all orgs where you are Owner or Admin. The repo records two Free Supabase projects already (levelup-crm laxxqmtwowitopbqnejs, email-automation haroonvfx-outreach bnivytzudrpjlscwdxuh; read from project CLAUDE.md, not checked in the dashboard). A third project for the Database app therefore needs a Pro org, or reuse of an existing project, or a different design. Pro org plus a Free org for the other two is allowed and documented.
providers.has_auth_realtime_cron: Unchanged by upgrade.
providers.sql_postgres: Postgres, unchanged.
providers.backups: Daily backups begin after the upgrade.
providers.commercial_use_ok: Yes.
providers.fit_for_this_app: Good: start on Free with the Database project in its own Free org ONLY if a free slot is available; otherwise create a new org on Pro for the Database app (about $25/month) and keep CRM and Outreach free in the other org. No data migration needed when upgrading later.

providers.provider: Supabase: extra accounts or organisations for more free projects (question 2)
providers.plan: Free, multiple organisations or multiple accounts
providers.free_storage: Documented hard rule: 2 active free projects in total across ALL organisations where you are Owner or Admin; paused projects do not count. The docs themselves allow two Free orgs with one project each. Because the DB quota is evaluated per org (summed over its projects), two free projects in two separate orgs give two separate 500 MB quotas, about 1 GB combined, but the data would be split across two projects (two Auth systems, no cross-project RLS, joins or Realtime).
providers.expiry_pause_or_deletion: Terms: the Acceptable Use Policy (Version 1, 1 June 2026) section 4.2 prohibits creating accounts in bulk or by automation and also prohibits maintaining an "excessive number of accounts as a single user" without Supabase's explicit permission; no number is defined for excessive. The AUP says violations can lead to immediate suspension or termination of the accounts and services (from a search summary, not read verbatim). The Terms of Service page has no multiple-account or free-tier clause (only general suspension for fraud, breach of the use restrictions, and non-payment). Fair Use restrictions (402, pausing, read-only) apply per organisation.
providers.other_free_limits: Creating accounts only to multiply free quota looks contrary to the two-free-project rule and AUP section 4.2; an account ban would take production data offline. Separate accounts for two real admins are not clearly covered, but using them to dodge the quota is a gray area: ask Supabase support for written permission before relying on it.
providers.has_auth_realtime_cron: Per project, not shared across projects.
providers.sql_postgres: Postgres per project.
providers.backups: None on Free.
providers.commercial_use_ok: Not stated for multi-account use.
providers.fit_for_this_app: Not recommended as the plan. The only clean use is one legit second Free project (in its own org) as an archive database for old leads, accepting the split. It is not worth the risk or complexity compared with $25/month for 8 GB.

providers.provider: Supabase: ways to get more than 500 MB free (question 7)
providers.plan: Promotions, startup, student, open-source programs, spend cap
providers.free_storage: No official route found. Startup credits: the supabase.com/solutions/startups page has no program, credit amount or application; one tracker (30 Oct 2026) says the old $300 / 6 months Pro offer is discontinued, while aggregator sites still list it (amounts conflict: $300, $2,500, $3,000), so treat as unverified. Student: no official program found; GitHub discussion 29381 (Sep 2024) has no staff confirmation. Open source: no official credits program found. One-off promos (e.g. a free Pro month via a podcast form) are not verified. Spend cap: exists only on Pro, protects from surprise bills, does not add free storage.
providers.expiry_pause_or_deletion: n/a
providers.other_free_limits: Ask Supabase support directly if the agency qualifies for a startup or sponsorship deal; do not plan around it.
providers.has_auth_realtime_cron: n/a
providers.sql_postgres: n/a
providers.backups: n/a
providers.commercial_use_ok: n/a
providers.fit_for_this_app: Do not count on any of these. Plan = Free until about 350 MB, then Pro.

providers.provider: Supabase: shrinking DB size (question 6: pruning, partitioning, TOAST compression)
providers.plan: Techniques, no plan change (work on Free or Pro)
providers.free_storage: Pruning: delete old rows, then vacuum; Supabase docs say deleted space is not reclaimed at once, VACUUM FULL <table> rewrites and locks that table, and disks do not shrink on their own (disk size only resets through an upgrade or migration). Partitioning: native range partitions by month; dropping or detaching an old partition is much faster than a bulk DELETE and avoids its VACUUM overhead (Postgres docs). Supabase documents a pg_partman page (create schema partman, create extension, schedule run_maintenance_proc via pg_cron), but a supabase/postgres issue (1586) says it was missing, so check the Extensions list; native partitions plus a small pg_cron function work either way. Housekeeping: cron.job_run_details is never auto-cleaned, so schedule a daily delete of rows older than 7 days (Supabase quickstart); a 1-minute job writes 1,440 rows a day. TOAST compression: text and jsonb are compressed automatically (pglz) but only when a row exceeds about 2 kB, so small lead rows gain little; per-column lz4 (Postgres 14+) is optional and works only if the server was built with lz4 (not verified on Supabase: test SET COMPRESSION lz4), and only affects newly written values.
providers.expiry_pause_or_deletion: n/a
providers.other_free_limits: Biggest real savings for this app (my judgment, not a sourced claim): store normalised columns instead of a raw jsonb copy of each sheet row, store a row hash for change detection, drop unused indexes, keep change history as diffs, archive old or closed leads as gzipped files in the 1 GB bucket, and prune sync logs and audit rows on a retention schedule.
providers.has_auth_realtime_cron: pg_cron runs the pruning and partition jobs.
providers.sql_postgres: Standard Postgres features.
providers.backups: Take a dump before any large delete.
providers.commercial_use_ok: n/a
providers.fit_for_this_app: Worth doing from day one (retention policy, log cleanup, monthly partitions for sync-event tables). It stretches Free but cannot make a growing lead table stay under 500 MB forever; combine with a Pro switch point.

providers.provider: Self-hosted Supabase (Docker Compose) on Hetzner Cloud CX23
providers.plan: Hetzner CX23: 2 vCPU, 4 GB RAM, 40 GB NVMe, 20 TB traffic. About EUR 5.99/month excl. VAT with IPv4 (EUR 5.49 without; roughly EUR 7.1 with 19% German VAT, my calculation). Prices rose twice in 2026 (latest 15 Jun 2026). Hetzner Backups add 20% of the server price (about EUR 1.2) for 7 slots.
providers.free_storage: 40 GB disk total, shared by OS, Docker images and Postgres data, so realistically about 20-25 GB for data (my estimate), versus 500 MB on Free. Supabase's minimum is 4 GB RAM, 2 cores, 40 GB SSD; recommended 8 GB+ RAM, 4 cores, 80 GB. CX33 (4 vCPU, 8 GB, 80 GB) is about EUR 8.99 incl. IPv4.
providers.expiry_pause_or_deletion: No pause or expiry; billed hourly with a monthly cap. AVAILABILITY WARNING: the hetzner.com cost-optimized page showed CX23 and the ARM CAX11 as currently unavailable on 2026-11-04, and one review says CX23 was unorderable in Oct 2026; the nearest orderable plan then was CPX22 (2 vCPU, 4 GB, 80 GB) at about EUR 19.99. Check the console before planning around EUR 6.
providers.other_free_limits: What you take on (official self-hosting overview): backups and disaster recovery (nothing built in, no PITR), security hardening, OS and Docker patching, monitoring and uptime, HTTPS reverse proxy, scaling. Support is community only. Missing vs hosted: branching, managed backups and PITR, Management API, multi-project Studio; Studio is protected only by shared basic auth, so anyone with the URL and password is admin. Updates: stable snapshots about monthly with an update.sh script, but upgrades are the most-cited pain point in the Supabase self-hosting thread (breaking changes, thin changelogs) and compatibility of mixed image tags is not guaranteed. Effort estimate (mine; no source quantifies it): about 1 day to build a hardened setup with TLS, firewall and tested backups, then 1-3 hours a month; the docs' under-15-minutes claim is a laptop test.
providers.has_auth_realtime_cron: Stack includes Studio, gateway, Auth, PostgREST, Realtime, Storage, Postgres, Edge Runtime (Deno; functions go in volumes/functions and need a restart), Supavisor. Same RLS behaviour. Realtime and Edge work per user reports, with slower cold starts. pg_cron and pg_net are not mentioned on the official Docker page: availability in the self-hosted Postgres image is NOT verified; test first, or fall back to host crontab calling the Edge Function every minute.
providers.sql_postgres: Same Postgres 15/17 image family and the same SQL, RLS, Auth and Realtime APIs as the hosted service, so the CRM/Outreach code would work unchanged apart from the URL and keys.
providers.backups: None built in. Build a nightly pg_dump -Fc via docker exec, keep .env, docker-compose.yml and volumes/functions, ship off-site, run restore drills. Add Hetzner Backups (20%) as a second layer.
providers.commercial_use_ok: Yes (own server). Supabase's Apache-2.0-style self-host licensing not checked.
providers.fit_for_this_app: Gives near-unlimited storage for about EUR 7-9/month, but the user would be the DBA for the agency's lead data with no vendor support. For about 5 users and 11 sheets, data volume is small, so this is not needed until data passes roughly 8 GB or $25/month is a blocker. Rank: Free + pruning first, Pro second, self-host last.

providers.provider: Self-hosted Supabase on Oracle Cloud Always Free (Ampere A1)
providers.plan: Always Free, $0. Ampere A1 allowance was cut on 15 Jun 2026 from 4 OCPU / 24 GB to 2 OCPU / 12 GB (1,500 OCPU-hours and 9,000 GB-hours a month) with no announcement; older tutorials are out of date.
providers.free_storage: 200 GB combined boot and block volume per tenancy (boot volume minimum 47-50 GB), 20 GB object storage, 2 OCI AMD micro VMs (1 GB RAM, too small for the stack). 12 GB RAM is enough for the full Supabase stack.
providers.expiry_pause_or_deletion: Idle policy: Always Free VMs may be reclaimed if, over 7 days, 95th-percentile CPU is under 20% and network is under 20% (and memory under 20% on A1). Instances above the new caps on free-only accounts are shut down until resized; one guide says they are deleted after 30 days. Whether pay-as-you-go accounts keep 4 OCPU / 24 GB at no charge is unclear (conflicting support answers). New A1 VMs often fail with out-of-capacity errors.
providers.other_free_limits: Self-hosting duties are the same as on Hetzner (backups, patching, uptime, security). ARM64 risk: a 2023-24 issue (supabase 18815, closed) shows the Vector (logging) container failing on Oracle ARM64 with an unsupported page size error; the workaround was to remove that service. Whether current official images are fully multi-arch was not verified: check with docker buildx imagetools inspect.
providers.has_auth_realtime_cron: Same stack as above; pg_cron and pg_net availability not verified.
providers.sql_postgres: Same Postgres and APIs as hosted Supabase.
providers.backups: None built in; Oracle includes 5 volume backups in the Always Free allowance.

supa.notes:
SHORT ANSWERS (checked 2026-11-04).
1) Past 500 MB on Free: nothing is deleted. Current official docs say 500 MB is a billing quota per organisation, not the read-only trigger. Over quota you get a grace period (length not published; user notices show about 2-3 weeks), then a Fair Use restriction: HTTP 402 on every API request for all projects in the org, judged on the AVERAGE daily size for the billing cycle. Read-only is a different trigger (95% of the fixed 2 GB Free disk; Postgres stops at 100%). Docs said read-only at 500 MB until a fix on 13 Apr 2026, and some blogs still say so, so plan for both. You can keep running during grace; after it, the app is down until the cycle resets, you upgrade to Pro, or you turn off the Pro spend cap.
2) Extra accounts or orgs: the docs cap free projects at 2 in total across all orgs you own or administer. The Acceptable Use Policy (Version 1, 1 June 2026) section 4.2 bars an "excessive number of accounts as a single user" without Supabase's explicit permission; no number is given and the Terms of Service page has no such clause. Two Free orgs with one project each is documented and legal (separate 500 MB quotas) but splits the data. Using more accounts to dodge limits: not recommended.
3) Storage: 1 GB free, 50 MB per file, separate from the DB quota. Nightly compressed dumps fit if split to 45 MB or less; roughly 7 days of snapshots. Compression ratio is an estimate; measure it.
4) Pro: from $25/month per org; 8 GB DB disk per project (then $0.125/GB), 100 GB storage, daily backups kept 7 days, no pausing, $10 compute credit covers one Micro project; extra projects about $10 each; PITR about $100/month extra; going past 8 GB needs the spend cap off.
5) In place: yes. Upgrade the organisation in billing settings; the same project keeps its data. All projects in that org become Pro, so keep other projects in a separate Free org via Project Transfers. Plan-switch downtime is not stated officially.
6) Shrinking: retention deletes plus vacuum, monthly partitions that are dropped, a daily cleanup of cron.job_run_details, and avoiding raw jsonb copies. TOAST compresses only rows over about 2 kB, so small lead rows gain little.
7) More free than 500 MB: no verified official program (startup credits appear discontinued; no student or open-source program found). Spend cap is Pro only.
SELF-HOST: Hetzner CX23 about EUR 6 plus VAT/IPv4 gives 40 GB, same Auth/RLS/Realtime/Edge stack, but the user owns backups, updates, security and uptime; the plan was shown as unavailable on Hetzner's page today. Oracle Always Free is now 2 OCPU / 12 GB (halved in June 2026), has an idle-reclaim rule and ARM image risk.
KEY FLAG: the CRM and Outreach apps already use the 2 Free Supabase projects per the repo notes (not checked in the dashboard), so the Database app cannot be a third Free project on that account. Options: new Pro org (about $25/month) for the Database app with CRM/Outreach kept free in another org, or put the app inside an existing project (shares that project's org quota).
NOT CHECKED / SKIPPED: exact grace-period length; whether a 1-minute pg_cron job counts as activity against the 1-week pause; pg_partman and lz4 availability on Supabase; pg_cron, pg_net and arm64 status in the self-hosted images; Oracle Free Tier commercial terms; EUR conversions for USD prices; real compression ratio of this app's dumps. Several sources are third-party blogs or GitHub user posts and are labelled as such.

decision.recommendation: Stay on the Supabase stack; no vendor switch. The data lives in a Supabase project in its OWN organisation (so a quota breach can never 402 the CRM): Free if the dashboard shows a free project slot, otherwise a new Pro org at $25/month for Database alone while CRM and Outreach stay in a Free org. The mirror is LEAN (30 typed fields per lead, no jsonb copy of the sheet row); the Google Sheets remain the permanent raw archive, so Suburb, Postcode, Map URL, Full Address, Lead Insight, Pitch Angle, Website Summary, YT/IG metrics and the other 40-odd columns stay only in the sheets and are re-read on demand or after any loss; only app-owned state (assignments, notes, tags, requests, reach events, audit) is irreplaceable and is small. Pruning from day one by pg_cron: audit kept 90 days, sync_log 30 days (and written only on change or error), cron.job_run_details 7 days, status history in the slim 129 B lead_status_event table, trigram index deferred until about 50k rows, VACUUM after each prune and REINDEX after the backlog import. Snapshots: nightly pg_dump -Fc of the app-owned tables only (not the rebuildable lead mirror) into the free 1 GB Storage bucket (under 50 MB per file, 7 kept) plus one weekly copy outside Supabase, and a restore drill before launch. Move to Pro when the 7-day average pg_database_size passes 350 MB (alert at 300), when daily backups or no-pause become a business need, or on day one if there is no free slot; the upgrade is in place with no migration.

decision.plain_answer_for_user:
With 4-5 employees and every lead assigned to someone, the assignment itself costs almost nothing (one small column per lead). What fills the database is the activity log and the scan log, not the leads. At your bot's volume (about 10,000 leads in month one, then about 2,500 a month) the lean design holds roughly 200 MB after a year if old logs are trimmed automatically (audit 90 days, scan log 30 days), so the free 500 MB lasts about 7 years. Without trimming it fills in about 7 months.

A free 1 GB database that also gives you login, per-sheet access, live counters and the 1-minute scanner does not exist. Neon offers 1 GB but its free compute runs out around day 17 each month with a scanner that never sleeps; the rest are bare databases, expire, or need a full rewrite. Not worth the switch.

Decision: Supabase, lean mirror, automatic log trimming, nightly backup of the app's own data to the free file store. One catch: Free allows 2 projects and the CRM and Outreach may already use both. If so, Database goes into its own Pro org at $25/month (8 GB, daily backups, no pausing).
